Q: Why is there no SortedList in Java? A:

SequencedCollection

Java 21 added sequenced collections to the Java Collections Framework. See JEP 431, and see talks by Stuart Marks.

Notice that List is now a sub-interface of SequencedCollection, to represent the notion that elements of the collection are iterated in a certain sequence.

SequencedCollection < String > names = List.of( "Carol" , "Alice", "Bob" ) ;

This new interface brings handy methods for accessing first/last elements, and a method to reverse the elements.

IO.println( "First: " + names.getFirst() + " | Last: " + names.getLast() ;

That does not change the fact that the sequence of a List is arbitrary, not sorted. You can place particular elements of a list in any particular slot. As noted in the Question, if you want them sorted, you can call Collections.sort for natural order if the elements’ class implements Comparable. Otherwise, include a Comparator to do the sorting. Tip: In Java 8+, you directly call sort on the List itself rather than going through Collections utility class. Be aware that the sequence continues to be arbitrary; the sorting is not maintained as you edit the list.

List < String > names = new ArrayList<>( List.of( "Carol" , "Alice", "Bob" ) ) ;
names.sort( null ) ;  // Passing `null` rather than `Comparator` means natural-order. Sorts just this once, not continually.

names.toString(): [Alice, Bob, Carol]

List interchangeable with SortedSet

Look at that class diagram above. Notice that SortedSet/NavigableSet, and LinkedHashSet, all implement SequencedCollection alongside List.

It is generally best to refer to your collections with the most general interface that meets the needs of your situation. If your needs are met by the interface contract promised by SequencedCollection, then use it. And if you do so, it means you can later switch between any of the classes implementing SequencedCollection.

For example, you may start with a quick List such as List.of( "Carol" , "Alice", "Bob" ). Eventually, you realize that you want those organized alphabetically while eliminating duplicates. That qualifies their use in a SequencedSet like TreeSet. You can just switch from List to TreeSet without changing related code because TreeSet’s super-interface SequencedSet is a sub-interface of SequencedCollection.

First you write:

SequencedCollection < String > names = List.of( "Carol" , "Alice", "Bob" ) ;

Later you change the code, to swap out List for TreeSet, without breaking any related code.

SequencedCollection < String > names = new TreeSet<>( List.of( "Carol" , "Alice", "Bob" ) ) ;  // Swapped out `List` for `TreeSet` without breaking code.

Choosing a sequenced collection

Here are some of the classes implementing SequencedCollection.

Class Purpose
ArrayList Hold items in arbitrary sequence. Good when usually reading or appending. Allows duplicates. Sorting possible, but not maintained.
LinkedList Hold items in arbitrary sequence. Good when often inserting/removing/swapping various elements. Allows duplicates. Sorting possible, but not maintained.
TreeSet Keeps elements in natural-order, or in Comparator order. Eliminates duplicates. Sorting maintained as you edit the collection.
ConcurrentSkipListSet Keeps elements in natural-order, or in Comparator order. Eliminates duplicates. Good for concurrent modification. Also good for rapidly adding/accessing large numbers of elements. Sorting maintained as you edit the collection.
LinkedHashSet Keeps elements in insertion-order. Eliminates duplicates.

Be aware of more classes implementing SequencedCollection, those classes implementing Deque: ArrayDeque, ConcurrentLinkedDeque, LinkedBlockingDeque, (& LinkedList).
